title: When to Prune Fruit Trees in South Australia: A Horticulturist's Month-by-Month Calendar
metaTitle: When to Prune Fruit Trees in SA: Month by Month Guide
excerpt: Month-by-month guide to pruning apples, pears, stone fruit, citrus, figs and olives in Adelaide, and the one mistake that costs you next year's crop.
imageAlt: Fruit tree pruned in winter in an Adelaide eastern suburbs backyard by Garden Grit horticulturist
bodyHtml:
Most of the fruit trees I prune in Adelaide's eastern suburbs have been cut at the wrong time of year, usually because someone had a free Saturday in October. The tree survives, but the crop does not. Here is the calendar I work to for fruit tree pruning in Adelaide, with the reasoning, so you can do the light work yourself and know when to call me for the rest.

The rule that covers most of it

Deciduous fruit trees are pruned when they are dormant or just after they have finished fruiting; evergreen fruit trees are pruned lightly after the frost risk has passed. Stone fruit are the exception that catches people out: they are pruned in late summer, not winter, to keep bacterial canker and silver leaf out of the fresh cuts while the sap is still moving.

June and July: pome fruit and grapes

Apples, pears, quinces and nashi are pruned while fully dormant. Take out dead, diseased and crossing wood first, open the centre so air and light get in, and shorten last season's leaders by about a third. Spur-bearing apples are tidied, not hacked; most of the fruit forms on two-year-old wood. Grapes are cut back hard to two or three buds per spur on an established framework. Figs can be pruned now too, though they need little.

August: olives, pomegranates and the last of the dormant work

Finish any pome fruit you missed before bud burst. Olives are pruned now to open the canopy; they fruit on last year's growth, so do not strip every young shoot. Pomegranates get dead wood and suckers removed. This is also the last month to prune roses and Crepe Myrtles in the same garden.

September and October: hands off

Blossom and new growth. Pruning now removes the crop. The only cutting I do in spring is formative pruning on newly planted trees and removing frost-damaged tips once the risk has passed.

November to January: citrus, and summer pruning for size control

Citrus (lemons, limes, oranges, mandarins) are pruned lightly after the last frost and after the main flush, usually late spring: remove dead wood, water shoots below the graft and anything touching the ground. Keep the skirt lifted so fruit stays clean. Apples and pears that are getting too big can be summer pruned in December by shortening vigorous new shoots, which checks growth without stimulating the regrowth that a winter cut would.

February and March: stone fruit

Apricots, plums, peaches, nectarines and cherries are pruned straight after harvest while the weather is dry. Fresh cuts heal quickly in the warmth and the trees are far less likely to pick up the fungal and bacterial diseases that get into winter cuts in Adelaide's wet months. Peaches and nectarines fruit on one-year-old wood, so remove the wood that has fruited and keep the new growth. Apricots and plums fruit on spurs; thin and tidy, do not strip.

April and May: clean up and plan

Remove mummified fruit, rake and bin fallen leaves from any tree that had leaf curl, brown rot or black spot, and note which trees need major work in winter. If a tree has not been pruned in years, the restoration is staged over two or three winters rather than done in one brutal cut.

The one mistake to avoid

Lopping: cutting every branch back to a stub to make the tree smaller. The tree responds with a mass of weak, vertical regrowth, shades itself out, and fruits less. Size is controlled by selective thinning and summer pruning, not by decapitation. If a fruit tree is genuinely too big for its spot, that is a conversation worth having before the saw comes out.

Need it done properly?

title: How Much Does Tree Pruning Cost in Adelaide? What Actually Moves the Price
metaTitle: Tree Pruning Cost in Adelaide: What Moves the Price
excerpt: What decides the price of tree pruning in Adelaide: size, access, neglect, green waste and horticulturist versus arborist. How to get an accurate quote.
imageAlt: Small ornamental tree after pruning in a Campbelltown, Adelaide garden, showing clean cuts and open canopy
bodyHtml:
Tree pruning in Adelaide is quoted per job, not off a price list, and that frustrates people who just want a number. The honest answer is that two trees of the same species in the same suburb can cost very different amounts to prune, and this post explains why so you can read a quote properly.

What the price is made of

Every quote I write for pruning is built from the same five things.

1. Size and height of the tree

A two-metre Crepe Myrtle pruned from the ground is a short job. A five-metre plum that needs a platform ladder and a pole saw is a half-day. Anything that needs climbing, rigging or a cherry picker is arborist work and is priced accordingly, usually by a different business.

2. How long since it was last pruned

A tree that is pruned every year takes a fraction of the time of one that has been left for a decade. Restoration pruning on a neglected tree is often staged over two or three visits, which costs more in total but gives you a tree worth keeping.

3. Access

Can the tree be reached with a ladder on firm ground? Is it against a fence, over a pool, or hemmed in by a shed? Narrow side access in the older streets of Norwood and St Peters, or a steep block in Athelstone, add time to both the pruning and the clean up.

4. Green waste

Removing and disposing of the prunings is part of the price. A big reduction on a mature tree generates a trailer load or more. If you have a green bin and are happy to take some yourself, say so and the quote will reflect it.

5. Horticulturist or arborist

For fruit trees, ornamentals and small to medium trees, a qualified horticulturist is the right person and the economical one. For large trees, anything near power lines, or trees that may be regulated or significant under South Australian planning law, you need a qualified arborist, and you should expect a higher price for the equipment and the insurance that goes with that work.

Why the cheap quote is usually a lopping quote

If one quote is far lower than the others, it is often because the plan is to cut everything back to stubs. That is fast, and it is also the worst thing you can do to the tree. Lopped trees regrow faster and weaker, need more frequent cutting and often end up removed. Ask any pruner what cuts they intend to make and why, and whether the tree will keep a natural shape.

How to get an accurate quote

  • Say what the tree is, or send a photo. Species changes the technique and the timing.
  • Tell the pruner what you want: more light, less height, fruit at picking height, clearance from the roof.
  • Mention access and whether you have a green bin.
  • Ask for the price to include clean up and removal.

Rough price bands

Without seeing the tree I will not put a number on it, but the shape of the pricing is simple. A single small ornamental or fruit tree pruned annually is a short visit with a modest fixed price. Three or four trees in the same garden on the same day cost less per tree than three separate visits. A neglected tree that needs staged restoration is quoted per stage. Anything that needs an arborist is a different conversation and a different price, and I will tell you if that is where your tree sits rather than pretending it is a job for a ladder.

I quote tree pruning in Magill, Campbelltown, Athelstone, Norwood, Burnside and across Adelaide's eastern suburbs after a quick site visit, and the number you get is the number you pay. See tree pruning or ask for a quote.

title: How Often Should You Trim a Hedge in Adelaide's Climate?
metaTitle: How Often to Trim a Hedge in Adelaide | Garden Grit
excerpt: How many times a year to trim Lilly Pilly, Photinia, Viburnum, Buxus, Murraya and Westringia hedges in Adelaide, when to do it and how hard to cut.
keyword: how often does a hedge need to be trimmed
imageAlt: Boundary hedge trimmed level and square in Walkerville, Adelaide by Garden Grit
bodyHtml:
How often a hedge needs trimming depends on what it is, how formal you want it and how much Adelaide's weather is pushing it along. The short answer for most formal hedges in the eastern suburbs is two to three times a year. The long answer is below, species by species, with the timing I use as a horticulturist.

Why Adelaide hedges grow in bursts

Our hedges put on a big flush in spring, slow or stop in the heat of January and February, grow again in autumn when the rain returns, and sit still through winter. Trimming after each flush keeps a hedge dense; trimming during the heat stresses it and exposes the inside to sunburn. So the calendar matters more than the number of cuts.

A trimming calendar for common hedges

HedgeTrims per yearBest timingNotes
Lilly Pilly (Syzygium, Acmena)3 to 4Late winter, early summer, autumnFast; trim after each flush. Watch for psyllid pimples on new growth.
Photinia 'Red Robin'3 to 4Spring, summer, autumnTrim to encourage the red new growth. Takes hard cuts.
Viburnum2 to 3After flowering, then autumnTrim too early and you lose the flowers.
Murraya2 to 3After each flowering flushFragrant flowers; trim lightly and often rather than hard.
Buxus (box)2Late spring, late summerSlow. Never trim in full sun on a hot day.
Pittosporum2 to 3Spring, autumnTolerates hard pruning; keep the top narrower than the base.
Westringia2After floweringNative; do not cut into bare old wood.
Conifers1 to 2Spring, late summerOnly trim green growth. Old wood will not reshoot.

How hard can you cut?

Broadleaf hedges like Lilly Pilly, Photinia, Viburnum and Pittosporum can be cut back hard and will regrow from old wood, which is how an overgrown hedge is rescued. Conifers, Lavender, Rosemary and most Westringia cannot; cut them into bare wood and that section stays bare. If a hedge has got away from you, a horticulturist will stage the reduction so there is always foliage left to feed the plant.

Signs you have left it too long

  • The hedge is wider at the top than the bottom and the base has gone thin and bare.
  • You can see through it in winter.
  • It has pushed over a path, fence line or driveway sightline.
  • Flowering hedges have stopped flowering because they are cut at the wrong time.

The trick to a dense hedge

Taper. Keep the top slightly narrower than the base so sunlight reaches the lower leaves, and the hedge stays green to the ground. Most hedges in Walkerville, Prospect and Toorak Gardens that have gone bare at the bottom were cut plumb or wider at the top for years.

Trimming in a heatwave

One more timing rule that matters in Adelaide: do not trim a hedge in the days before or during a run of 35-degree days. Freshly cut leaves and the newly exposed inner foliage scorch, and a hedge that looked fine on Monday is brown on the sunny side by Friday. If the forecast is hot, the trim waits a week. Water the hedge well the day before any trim in summer and again afterwards.

I trim hedges across Norwood and Adelaide's eastern suburbs on a schedule that suits the species. See hedge trimming or book a quote.

title: Lawn Installation Cost in Adelaide: Kikuyu, Buffalo & Couch Compared
metaTitle: Lawn Installation Cost Adelaide: Kikuyu vs Buffalo vs Couch
excerpt: What goes into the cost of a new lawn in Adelaide, how Kikuyu, Buffalo and Couch compare, and why preparation is where the money is well spent.
imageAlt: New roll-on lawn laid by Garden Grit between garden beds at a Norwood, Adelaide property
bodyHtml:
People ask what a new lawn costs per square metre, and the turf price is the smallest part of the answer. The real cost of lawn installation in Adelaide is in what happens before the rolls arrive. This guide breaks the job into its parts, compares the three turf types that suit Adelaide, and explains where it is worth spending.

The parts of a lawn installation

  1. Removal. Old lawn, weeds, builders' rubble on new sites. The more there is to take out, the more it costs.
  2. Soil. A new lawn needs 100 mm or more of good sandy loam over the existing ground, improved with organic matter. Skip this and the lawn struggles on Adelaide's clay every summer.
  3. Levelling and compaction. A gentle fall away from the house, no hollows, a fine finish.
  4. Irrigation. Pop-up sprinklers or sub-surface drip, installed before the turf so the lawn gets water evenly from day one.
  5. Turf. Priced per square metre, delivered on pallets, and laid the day it arrives.
  6. Laying and aftercare. Rolls laid brickwork-fashion, rolled, watered in, with a watering and first-mow schedule.

Kikuyu, Buffalo and Couch compared

KikuyuSoft-leaf BuffaloCouch
Turf priceLowestHighestMid
Shade tolerancePoorGoodPoor
Wear and recoveryExcellentGoodGood
Winter colourFairGoodBrowns off
Water needsModerateModerate to lowLow
MowingFrequent in summerFortnightlyFrequent, low cut
InvasivenessRuns into bedsContainedRuns
Best forFull-sun family yards, Tea Tree Gully and Golden Grove new buildsPart-shade established gardens in Norwood, Burnside, MagillFull-sun show lawns

Kikuyu is the budget workhorse: cheap, tough, fast to establish, and it will take a football. It will also invade your garden beds, so it needs edging. Soft-leaf Buffalo (Sir Walter and similar) costs more per square metre but copes with the dappled shade of the established eastern-suburbs gardens, stays greener in winter and stays where you put it. Couch gives the finest, tightest surface but wants full sun, a low regular mow and goes brown in winter unless you oversow.

Where the money is well spent

If the budget is tight, spend it on soil and irrigation and choose Kikuyu, rather than buying Buffalo and laying it on unimproved clay with no watering system. A cheaper turf on good preparation beats a premium turf on bad preparation every time.

Timing affects the price too

Spring and autumn are the easiest times to establish a lawn in Adelaide, and turf farms are busiest in spring. Laying in summer works but needs more water and more attention. Winter laying is slow to knit. I avoid laying during heatwaves entirely.

Questions to ask before you accept a quote

  • How deep is the soil being brought in, and what is it?
  • Is the old lawn and any rubble being removed, or just covered?
  • Is irrigation included, and is it going in before the turf?
  • Which turf variety, and from which farm?
  • Does the price include laying, rolling, watering in and the aftercare schedule?

A quote that cannot answer these is a quote for the turf, not for a lawn.

I install lawns across Tea Tree Gully, Modbury, Golden Grove, Norwood and Adelaide's eastern suburbs, with the irrigation in first. See turf installation or get a quote, and mention the size of the area and how much sun it gets.
